worker_target_description: Adult female Sprague Dawley offspring exposed prenatally to DEX versus CON, postnatally blood-sampled under restraint, tested for basal ASR at 6–7 months. Page 447 section 3.1 contains an overall prenatal-exposure test and separate light- and dark-phase nested-litter tests; supplied locator does not specify which.
worker_notes: Only assigned unfinished fields n_r and reported_success were examined for completion; original side and replication es/p are unassigned placeholders. Candidate basal-ASR tests on p. 447: overall prenatal DEX effect F(1,70) = 7.520; P = 0.008; light-phase DEX versus CON, pups nested within litter, F(1,28) = 5.963; P = 0.021; dark-phase DEX versus CON, pups nested within litter, F(1,28) = 3.462; P = 0.073. These are separate tests, not interchangeable effect/p pairs. No candidate selected by row order or numeric matching. Candidate animal N: 20 CON + 17 DEX = 37 distinct female offspring. Prenatal CON and DEX are mutually exclusive groups. The same set of offspring was tested in light and dark phases, so phase totals must not be added as independent animals. Fig. 1 confirms n = 17–20 per plotted group. Five CON and four DEX litters are separately reported (9 litters, not 9 animals). No ASR-specific animal exclusions are stated in the inspected methods/results; the 24 time-mated females are mothers, and the molecular-analysis subsamples are not the ASR sample. No N was inferred from degrees of freedom. Candidate N retained here for parent field-scope review because the locator does not resolve the intended test. Authors explicitly call the light-phase result a replication of reference [9], which is the assigned Hougaard et al. (2005) paper, so reported_success is successful as an author narrative verdict, independently of statistical target ambiguity. Rendered and inspected supplied PDF pages 445, 447, 448; canonical text used for all quotes.

coding_context.description: Prenatal exposure to the synthetic glucocorticoid dexamethasone (or to chronic mild stress) leads to a heightened acoustic startle response (ASR) in adult rat offspring.
coding_context.reported_success_quote:
We hereby replicated our earlier findings in a new strain and
laboratory, thus strengthening the validity of our model regarding prenatal stress effects on ASR in female
offspring.

prior_adjudication.location: Printed p. 447 / PDF page 4, Section 3.1 Basal startle; Printed p. 448 / PDF page 5, Section 4 Discussion
prior_adjudication.quote: When analyzed separately for the light and the dark phases, basal … startle was significantly increased in DEX compared to CON offspring … during the light phase ([F(1,28) = 5.963; P = 0.021]; tested with pups … nested within litter). Basal ASR also seemed increased in DEX … compared to CON offspring when tested during the dark phase, … although this difference did not reach statistical significance at p b 0.05 … ([F(1,28) = 3.462; P = 0.073]; tested with pups nested within litter).
prior_adjudication.reason: The neutral locator (p. 447, prenatal dexamethasone effect on adult offspring acoustic startle response) does not uniquely distinguish among the overall two-way ANOVA main effect across diurnal phases ("DEX: F(1,70) = 7.520; P = 0.008"), the nested-litter light-phase comparison ("[F(1,28) = 5.963; P = 0.021]"), and the non-significant nested-litter dark-phase comparison ("[F(1,28) = 3.462; P = 0.073]"). Although the authors state that the study "replicates our earlier ﬁnding of increased basal startle in blood sampled animals, prenatally exposed to DEX and tested during light phase [9]" and "replicated our earlier ﬁndings in a new strain and laboratory," the unresolved target test prevents confirming an effect-specific replication verdict without relying on numeric coincidence.
